system:
You are shown a snapshot of US macroeconomic and market data as it was known at the end of one month between 2007 and 2026.

Estimate which month the snapshot describes. Use only the figures supplied plus your general knowledge of economic history.

Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"year": yyyy, "month": m, "confidence": c, "cues": ["...", "..."]}
Rules: year is an integer from 2007 to 2026; month is an integer from 1 to 12; c in [0, 1] is your confidence that the guess is within 6 months of the truth; 1 to 3 short cues citing the inputs.
text:
Key features: unemployment very low relative to the last 3 years (-2.0) and falling, strong payrolls, rising activity, credit spreads tight, VIX low, policy rate slightly below average (-0.5) but rising over 12m. 2-year yield above average. Headline CPI rising. Gold weak.

The 36-month window would be a period where the policy rate was lower earlier, then rising. Unemployment at a 3-year low with a 12m drop of -1.5 suggests recovery from a higher unemployment level. Candidates: late 2017 (unemployment falling to 4.1%, 3-year window includes 2014-2017 with a low policy rate, so the policy rate would be above average... plausibly +1). Policy rate -0.5 with a 12m change of +0.5 is odd. Maybe late 2016 to early 2017? In that case the policy rate would be around average. Alternatively 2022-2023? There the unemployment rate at 3.4% against a window including 2020-21 would be -2, and the policy rate would be high. Not a fit.

Another possibility: early 2005? Out of range. Late 2018? Unemployment 3.7%, policy rate high. Late 2024/early 2025: unemployment 4.1% against a window from 2022 (3.5%) to 2024 would be above average. No.

Late 2021: unemployment falling fast, but the policy rate was at zero, and the window would include 2019-2020. Not a fit.

Consider the 2-year yield at +1.0 while the policy rate is -0.5: the market is pricing hikes. This fits late 2016 or early 2017: the window is 2014-2017, the policy rate at 0.5-0.75 versus a mean of about 0.2... that would be positive. Hmm. Consider 2017 H2: the window of 2014-2017 has a policy rate mean of around 0.5, and a rate of 1.25 would be positive. Not -0.5.

Consider 2007: the window starts in 2004 with low rates, so the policy rate would be above average. Not a fit.

Consider late 2021/early 2022 with the window being 2019-2021: unemployment at 4.0% in January 2022 versus a window including 14% in April 2020 would give a mean of around 5.5, so z of about -1.5 to -2. The policy rate at 0.08 versus a mean of about 0.7 would give -0.5. The 2-year yield at 1.0 fits January 2022 (rising). Payrolls strong, headline CPI z of 0 is odd, though—CPI would be high. But CPI z is relative to the change in CPI... If the CPI is measured as a year-over-year rate, it would be a high z in 2022. Hmm, headline at 0 with +1 over 3m.

Alternatively, 2018: the window 2015-2018, policy rate mean of ~0.7, with a rate of 1.5-2.4 versus a mean of about 0.8, giving positive. No.

Consider 2023-2024... the policy rate would be high. Late 2019: rate 1.55 versus a 2016-2019 mean of 1.2 gives positive. Hmm.

Consider mid-2022 with a window of 2019-2022: no, since the CPI would be very high.

What about 2026? The window of 2023-2026 has a high policy rate, and the current rate at about 3.6% is below average, giving -0.5. But the 12m change would be negative. Not a fit.

Late 2016 (Nov/Dec): window of 2014-2016, policy rate mean of 0.2 and a rate of 0.5-0.66 giving a positive z. Not a fit.

I'll go with early 2022. The 10-year at +0.5 and falling over 3m doesn't fit, though. The 10-year fell in 2025... Alternatively, mid-2018? No. I'll choose January 2022 with low confidence.
